articles.title: SSR AI committee position statement: top 10 high-impact AI applications and value propositions for musculoskeletal radiologists.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Effective application of artificial intelligence (AI) in musculoskeletal (MSK) radiology depends on targeting unmet clinical needs rather than technical feasibility. This Society of Skeletal Radiology (SSR) position statement identifies and prioritizes the most impactful AI applications and value propositions for MSK radiologists. METHODS: The SSR AI Committee (n = 18) used structured brainstorming to compile lists of AI-based applications and value propositions. After deduplication, standardization, and categorization using a 12-component MSK radiology value cycle, refined lists were distributed as electronic surveys to 122 SSR committee members; 103 (84.4%) and 102 (83.6%) completed the applications and value propositions surveys, respectively, scoring each item on a 5-point Likert scale. Top 10 lists were generated from summed scores. RESULTS: Brainstorming generated 208 AI application and 126 value proposition ideas, condensed to 138 and 56 unique items, respectively. Fourteen AI applications and 13 value propositions shared the top 10 ranks (tied scores). Top-ranked AI applications were within dictation and reporting (5 items), archiving and presentation (2), diagnostic imaging (1), follow-up imaging (2), quality/safety (2), and protocoling (2). Top-ranked value propositions were within dictation and reporting (4), diagnostic imaging (3), ordering (3), protocoling (2), and quality/safety (1). The highest-ranked application was AI-assisted comparison study retrieval (mean 3.17/4.0) and the highest-ranked value proposition was increased reporting efficiency (mean 3.30/4.0). CONCLUSIONS: This position statement provides a demand-driven roadmap for AI development in MSK radiology. Workflow and reporting tools were prioritized over disease detection algorithms, highlighting a gap between clinical needs and current commercial AI offerings.

articles.title: Data drift in clinical imaging AI: Medicolegal liability after deployment.
articles.abstract: Data drift refers to changes in the distribution or characteristics of input data after deployment that may adversely affect the performance of artificial intelligence (AI) systems, even when the software continues to function exactly as designed. Patient demographics, disease prevalence, referral patterns, imaging protocols and technology continue to evolve after deployment, resulting in a divergence between the data distribution a model was trained on and the distribution it encounters in practice, without any discrete coding error or malfunction. These technical realities raise distinctive medicolegal questions when a patient is harmed by a degraded model. Establishing negligence centers on whether an ongoing institutional duty exists to monitor for performance deterioration, how breach can be proved absent consensus benchmarks for surveillance frequency and how causation can be demonstrated where AI output is only one element of clinical decision-making and its reasoning may be an opaque "black box" to its users. Comparative fault principles may allocate responsibility according to relative control and knowledge among institutions, vendors and radiologists. Products liability exposure and federal preemption laws also play a role. Risk reduction measures include lifecycle documentation, risk proportionate surveillance, auditability of algorithms and outputs, contractual allocation of monitoring responsibility, and sustained clinician oversight. Radiologists and institutions should anticipate a standard of care that evolves well before controlling case law develops.

articles.title: Can large language models (LLMs) be used to generate Fellowship of the Royal College of Radiologists (FRCR) Part 1 physics questions? A multimodel comparative reviewer-based study.
articles.abstract: AIM: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for medical examination support. However, evidence regarding their ability to generate Fellowship of the Royal College of Radiologists (FRCR) Part 1 Physics questions is limited. We compared the quality of questions generated by ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This was a comparative reviewer-based study. A total of 105 FRCR Part 1 Physics questions were analysed, with 35 questions from each source. Questions were equally sampled across 7 domains. Five independent reviewers scored each question and its rationale on a 10-point Likert scale for clarity, relevance, suitability and appropriateness, technical accuracy, difficulty level, adequacy of explanation, and reliability of rationale. The primary outcome was the overall combined reviewer-rated question quality score. Secondary analyses examined individual quality criteria, physics domains and inter-reviewer agreement. RESULTS: ChatGPT showed the highest overall mean score (8.28), followed by Gemini (8.14) and Perplexity (7.75). The overall source effect was statistically significant (P < .001). ChatGPT ranked first in all 7 domains. Gemini scored highest for clarity, while ChatGPT scored highest for relevance, suitability, technical accuracy, difficulty level, adequacy of explanation, and reliability of rationale. Across all models, relevance scored highest and difficulty level scored lowest. Reviewer severity varied significantly. CONCLUSION: Under the study conditions, ChatGPT received the highest overall reviewer ratings, followed by Gemini and Perplexity. LLMs may support supervised question generation and candidate revision, but the limited sample, reviewer variability and absence of psychometric validation require cautious interpretation. Human expert review remains essential.

articles.title: MSF-Fusion: A Mamba-driven spatial and frequency fusion network for multimodal medical images.
articles.abstract: Multimodal medical image fusion (MMIF) is important for accurate diagnosis and treatment. However, when striving for high spatial resolution and deep semantic alignment, challenges such as global semantic loss, feature redundancy, and reconstruction artifacts often arise. To address these issues, a Mamba-driven 2D image fusion network, MSF-Fusion, is proposed in this paper. First, the Local-Global Mamba Block (LGMB) serves as the core invertible transformation unit, striking a balance between local detail extraction and long-range dependency capture. Second, the Frequency Complementary Contrast (FCC) module extracts complementary cross-modal information while suppressing feature redundancy, supplemented by the Serial Mamba-Conv (SMC) module to achieve deep semantic integration and spatial recovery. Finally, the Adaptive Frequency Reconstruction Module (AFRM) mitigates artifacts by dynamically calibrating frequency energy while maintaining structural fidelity. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that MSF-Fusion exhibits certain advantages in both quantitative metrics and visual visualization, providing imaging support for clinical diagnosis and treatment.
